canberra.title: The Social Reckoning attempts to expose shady Facebook dealings but struggles with a flat narrative
canberra.snippet: The Social Network did what almost everyone thought was impossible: make Facebook’s creation exciting. Aaron Sorkin won an Academy ...
canberra.content:
18 October 2026

Start the conversation

Succession’s Jeremy Strong replaces Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning. Photo: Sony Pictures.

The Social Network did what almost everyone thought was impossible: make Facebook’s creation exciting.

Aaron Sorkin won an Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay, and since its 2011 release, many consider it one of the best-edited films of all time.

So while the story of how the world’s youngest-ever billionaire got sued by his closest friend and his meteoric rise due to the creation of Facebook was fantastic, does it really require an indirect sequel 15 years later?

Obviously Sony and Sorkin thought so, and now we have a film about the Facebook whistleblower leaking internal documents to The Wall Street Journal, detailing how the company knew it was exposing people to harmful content.

Best Actress winner Mickey Madison plays Frances Haugen, a Meta employee who joins Facebook hoping to bring the world together through social media.

She learns Meta has allowed harmful content, particularly on Instagram, to appear in users’ feeds because it correlates with higher retention rates. The content shown has also been linked with the worsening mental health of its users, specifically teenage girls.

Haugen then leaks the information to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), and the pair work to change how social media presents and filters news and content.

While The Social Reckoning is a companion piece to The Social Network, it is by no means a sequel. Zuckerberg isn’t the focus. It doesn’t retain any of the same actors, and aside from Sorkin writing and taking over from David Fincher to direct, a lot of the people behind the camera have changed.

The direction is less a retelling of events and more an investigative drama, creating an almost entirely different feel from the 2011 film.

This is where The Social Reckoning will lose people.

The film lacks David Fincher’s flair that made the 2011 movie so gripping. It feels more like a documentary than entertainment.

There aren’t any characters here. Everyone is just delivering info through exposition.

Whether you like Jesse Eisenberg or not, you can’t deny he was the centre of the first film, and his almost psychopathic delivery made audiences hate him. Add in Andrew Garfield as the naive Eduardo Savrin and Justin Timberlake as the weaselly Sean Parker, and you’ve got an iconic trio of characters.

That’s just not the case for The Social Reckoning. Everyone plays their roles almost exactly as you expect, which is fine but does little to elevate the movie’s emotion.

The plot doesn’t lend itself to a particularly interesting narrative. While the leak findings, the court outcomes and the lack of repercussions are all very shocking, they don’t form a narrative; they’re just scary facts.

The Social Reckoning is pretty underwhelming given the near-identical promotion it had to The Social Network.

Unfortunately, its quick, snappy, very Sorkin dialogue doesn’t do enough to make the story very interesting to watch.

While the impacts of social media on mental health and its role in spreading misinformation and disinformation need to be discussed, this film wasn’t skilful enough to pull it off.

The Social Reckoning is now showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: Who cares for Canberra’s 58,000 carers? New plan aims to ease the burden
canberra.snippet: Every day, thousands of Canberrans help loved ones get dressed, prepare meals, attend medical appointments or manage complex health condi...
canberra.content:
Around 58,000 Canberrans provide unpaid care to loved ones, often balancing their responsibilities with work, family life and their own wellbeing. Photo: Georgy Mathews.

Every day, thousands of Canberrans help loved ones get dressed, prepare meals, attend medical appointments or manage complex health conditions. Many juggle these responsibilities with jobs, studies and raising families. Some do not even think of themselves as carers.

But while their work allows others to live with dignity and independence, the toll on their own health and wellbeing often goes unnoticed.

With about 58,000 unpaid carers in the ACT, the government has released a new action plan to improve support, including exploring a dedicated respite and wellbeing hub and a recognition card to make accessing services easier.

The plan comes during National Carers Week, as new national figures reveal the emotional strain experienced by those looking after others.

The 2025 Carer Wellbeing Survey found that 61.1 per cent of carers reported low wellbeing, compared with 33.6 per cent of the general adult population. More than four in 10 carers reported loneliness, while almost one-third experienced high psychological distress.

The ACT Carers Strategy Final Action Plan 2026–2028 focuses on improving access to services, recognising unpaid carers, supporting young carers and strengthening coordination between services.

Among its proposals is an investigation into a purpose-built carer wellbeing and respite hub, offering the possibility of a dedicated space where carers could access support and take a break from their responsibilities.

The government will also explore a carer recognition card to help carers identify themselves when accessing services.

Other initiatives include updating information for foster and kinship carers and examining a mentoring program to help young carers continue their education and find employment.

Community Services Minister Caitlin Tough said carers made an enormous contribution to Canberra, but their responsibilities could come at a personal cost.

“While their contribution is invaluable, caring responsibilities can also have significant impacts on carers’ own health, wellbeing, employment, education and participation in community life,” Ms Tough said.

“That is why the ACT Government, in partnership with Carers ACT, remains focused on ensuring carers receive the recognition and support they need to thrive.”

However, several initiatives remain at the investigation or feasibility stage, with no confirmed delivery dates outlined in the material released.

For Carers ACT Board Chair Thilini Perera, recognising people who provide unpaid care is an important first step.

Many parents, partners, children and friends who care for someone with disability, chronic illness or age-related frailty simply see their responsibilities as part of family life.

Earlier this year, Carers ACT launched its Are You a Carer? campaign to help people recognise their caring roles and connect with available support.

The organisation is also encouraging workplaces, schools, health services and community organisations to become better at identifying carers who may be struggling.

“Recognition cannot be the responsibility of carers alone. We want our community to become better at identifying carers, understanding their needs and connecting them with support. Making carers visible is only the beginning – recognition must lead to meaningful support,” Ms Perera said.

She welcomed the government’s final action plan but emphasised the importance of delivering its commitments.

“These remain as relevant as ever for Canberra’s 58,000 carers, and we are keen to continue working with government and community to make sure they are delivered for carers.”

The challenges facing carers extend well beyond the ACT.

Across Australia, more than three million people provide unpaid care to family members and friends living with disability, chronic or terminal illness, mental health conditions or age-related frailty.

Their contribution is valued at an estimated $110 billion annually in replacement care costs, according to Carers Australia.

Yet behind that contribution are people who may struggle to find time for their own medical appointments, maintain friendships or remain in paid employment.

Feros Care project manager Ben Happ said the impact of carer exhaustion could extend beyond the individual to the people relying on them.

“When a carer becomes exhausted, isolated or unwell, the impact doesn’t stop with that individual. It affects the person relying on them, and ultimately the services around them. Supporting carers means looking after their wellbeing too, so they continue caring for people who depend on them without putting their own health at risk.”

Feros Care is encouraging Australians to offer practical help, whether through preparing meals, assisting with shopping, providing transport or giving carers a few hours to themselves.

Meanwhile, Carers ACT is marking National Carers Week with events including a gala dinner at the National Arboretum, a carers information pop-up, a gathering at Lanyon Homestead and a creative experiences day for young carers.

For more information, visit National Carers Week.

canberra.title: Holy Gods! I’ve been captured by romantasy and I don’t want saving (unless you have dark magic, wings or a dragon)
canberra.snippet: Dear readers, the strength it is costing me to write this column rather than explore another magical realm with a tall, dark, handsome st...
canberra.content:
Whilst always a little on the random side, my reading pile has splintered off in an unexpected direction. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Dear readers, the strength it is costing me to write this column rather than explore another magical realm with a tall, dark, handsome stranger is truly superhuman.

I may, in fact, be a fae warrior myself.

To be clear, fantasy is not my usual style. I grew up on Looking for Alibrandi and Hating Alison Ashley and matured into Bridget Jones and Stephanie Plum. I had a brief love affair with P.G. Wodehouse, and my favourite “comfort” reads are either Cold Mountain by Charles Frazier, or Harry Potter.

Basically, I’m all over the place. I’m “genre-fluid”.

But I’m also a millennial, which means I was raised by old school Disney, matured into Twilight, and ended up tragically addicted to social media.

It’s not surprising, therefore, that I’ve been sucked directly into romantasy’s vortex.

One of the fastest-growing genres of the book world, romantasy is what happens when you take classic formulaic romance like Mills & Boon, and throw it into a washing machine with the Twilight Series, Game of Thrones and Dungeons & Dragons.

And Millennials and Gen Z readers are riding that spin cycle, having the time of our lives.

The recent exponential growth of this curious genre is largely credited to #BookTok – a social media niche of user-generated content discussing, reviewing and recommending books.

To give you an idea, one of romantasy’s most iconic titles – and a common gateway drug for this addiction – Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses (referred to as ACOTAR) was first released in 2015, but it wasn’t until #BookTok took off that the series exploded in popularity.

This is how I ended up on my current quest through the nine realms of the cruel, magic-colonised continent of Emarion and Penn Cole’s Everflame series.

I may sound like a geek, but geeks did not lead me on this quest.

No, I was lured into this realm by a former Raiders player sharing book reviews from the cab of a tractor. Naturally.

One of the biggest names in the social zeitgeist, the ever-surprising Luke Bateman, is a professional athlete, media personality, mental health advocate and feminist, who has amassed an epic following for his love of literature, and particularly fantasy.

See? Cool people can like dragons, too.

If the romantasy Gods have not yet blessed you, allow me to give a short initiation.

I don’t want to trivialise the genre. Many of these novels are incredibly well-written, with vivid world-building, intricate plots, gripping story-telling and completely unleashed imaginations.

Many are also one long cliche. Held together by tropes. Threaded with cringe.

And I eat it up. Nom nom nom.

Firstly, our heroes are 18-years-old. In reality, this makes them babies with provisional licences, screen addictions, and still-developing brains. But in romantasy? They’re seasoned assassins with a dark past. Shhh.

Is that a bit weird? Yes. But as #BookTok-ers point out, if the heroes were our age their knees would give way in the first chapter.

Also, everyone’s name has entirely too many consonants, clustered together in an unpronounceable mess, like a cat has walked over the keyboard. Don’t bother trying. Just move on.

Our protagonist is always hyper-independent and strong-willed, whilst also being in desperate need of rescue.

Typically, she’s stuck in an inconceivably tragic situation with no way out. But fortunately, she always comes with at least one survival skill, in which she’s freakishly accomplished.

She’s impossibly poor, but feeds her family by hunting with deadly archery skill. She’s imprisoned and cruelly enslaved, but trained in martial arts thanks to a previous life as an assassin. You get the gist…

Next, the love story is enemies-to-lovers. Exclusively.

The unassuming – probably blonde – love interest who appears in the beginning? Yeah, he’s not it. And he better get ready, because about 700 pages in, he will be reduced to an utterly-disposable plot device, after our protagonist shares a long look with a dark, handsome stranger of questionable intent.

Of course, our protagonist and this really annoying stranger are then annoyingly drawn together to embark on a shared quest. There is simply no other solution. It’s honestly so annoying!

Oh, and on this journey, there is absolutely always only one room left available at the inn. How annoying!

Despite my pisstaking, I love my romantasy captors. They have helped me make time for reading and avoid life’s responsibilities by providing a hearty serve of escapism, immersion, and – okay – maybe a slightly unhealthy side of straight-up dissociation.

If you’re ready to be converted, genre-toppers include Sarah J Maas, Rebecca Yarros and Jennifer L Armentrout.

As for me, I must now return to my enslavement. Please don’t send help.

Unless he has dark magic, a foreboding nature and is, honestly, just so annoying.

canberra.title: Woman drowns after being hit by wave while rock fishing
canberra.snippet: A woman has died after being struck by a wave while rock fishing on the NSW South Coast. About 6pm Saturday 17 October 2026, emergency se...
canberra.content:
18 October 2026

18 October 2026

Start the conversation

A fisher has drowned at North Durras Beach on the NSW South Coast. Photo: Shoalhaven Tourism.

A woman has died after being struck by a wave while rock fishing on the NSW South Coast.

About 6pm Saturday 17 October 2026, emergency services were called to North Durras Beach, about 25 km north of Batemans Bay, after reports of two people in the water.

Officers from South Coast Police District responded along with NSW Ambulance paramedics, Surf Lifesavers, Fire and Rescue NSW Marine Rescue.

Police were told a 39-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman were rock fishing at the location when a wave struck the woman, knocking her into the surf.

The man entered the surf to retrieve her but was unable to do so and was washed back to shore.

A passing vessel found the woman and the crew dragged her from the water. She was returned to shore where CPR was performed, but the woman could not be revived and died at the scene.

Neither fisher was wearing safety equipment.

A report will be prepared for the information of the coroner.

Original Article published on About Regional.

canberra.title: Blokes searching for connection and community lace up their boots for The Man Walk
canberra.snippet: You don’t have to be a bloke or belong to a walking group to join the NSW Man Walker Camp in Crookwell next month. If you are looking for...
canberra.content:
The Man Walk offers a space for men to get together and find support. Photo: Facebook.

You don’t have to be a bloke or belong to a walking group to join the NSW Man Walker Camp in Crookwell next month. If you are looking for a place to talk, share your stories, and get out and about in relaxed company, this camp is for you.

Man Walk founder Mark Burns has built a charity based around a simple framework: Walk, Talk, Support.

The Man Walk provides free weekly walks for men in their local area. Starting as “just one man in Kiama”, it has now grown to 106 locations across Australia and the world.

In the ACT, there are two locations for walks in Tuggeranong, as well as one in the city.

There are also 42 locations in NSW, covering primarily regional and rural locations, where Mr Burns believes the service is most-needed.

“It’s really heartwarming to see how many blokes want to get together to catch up for a walk and a talk and share what’s going on in their life,” he said.

“You don’t need to have a problem to come for a walk. You don’t need to have a big conversation either. Sometimes you just need to get out of the house and spend a bit of time with other people.

“That regular catch-up can mean a lot. We want more men in regional communities to have that opportunity, and we want to keep it free.”

For those wanting more out of the experience, the NSW Man Walker Camp on Saturday 14 November provides participants with the opportunity to gather together, support regional communities, and enjoy a bacon and egg roll for breakfast.

“People hear ‘Man Walker Camp’ and might think it’s only for blokes who already walk with us. It’s not. Bring your partner, bring the kids, bring a mate. Everyone’s welcome,” Mr Burns said.

“We want people from Crookwell, Goulburn, Canberra and the surrounding communities to come along, have a good day and get behind something that matters.”

Beginning at 8:30 am, the Man Walker Camp starts with a 5 km community walk in the morning, followed by a barbecue breakfast.

There are activities in the afternoon at Meadowview Farm, with music in the evening and a spit roast dinner. Minibuses are available throughout the day for transport.

The day also includes the presentation of the NSW ‘Manbassador of the Year’ and the Greg Memorial Trophy.

The Man Walk is free for men to attend, and Mr Burns says it always will be, but it has been difficult to source government grants and sponsorships while juggling the costs of running a rapidly expanding organisation.

The $50 that people are asked to pay for attendance at the Man Walker Camp goes towards the meals and activities provided on the day, but also towards funding ongoing Man Walks across the state.

“Money raised from the camp will go directly back to regional and rural Man Walk locations,” Mr Burns said.

The Man Walk charity also provides mental health education, both face-to-face and virtually. This is free for Man Walkers and Man Walk supporters

Mr Burns said, beyond the Man Walker Camp, there were opportunities for men wanting to be involved to join the walks, interact with The Man Walk community, or even start new walks in their local area.

More information about The Man Walk can be found here. The Man Walker Camp will be held at Crookwell on Saturday 14 November Man Walker Camp and further details are here.

australia.title: ‘Many family stories’: Tim Winton’s Cloudstreet takes out ABC radio poll of top 100 Australian books
australia.snippet: Markus Zusak’s novel The Book Thief secures second place, while Trent Dalton’s Boy Swallows Universe rounds out podium dominated by men C...
australia.content:
Cloudstreet, Tim Winton’s sprawling Australian family epic, has been voted Australia’s favourite book in a poll run by ABC Radio National.

The broadcaster announced over the weekend the results of a nationwide poll to determine a list of readers’ top 100 Australian books.

Markus Zusak’s 2005 novel The Book Thief took second place, while Trent Dalton’s Boy Swallows Universe came in third.

First published in 1991, Cloudstreet follows two working-class Australian families, the Lambs and the Pickles, over their 20 years living together in an old rambling house called Cloudstreet, in postwar Perth.

The story – Winton’s fifth novel and ninth book – won a swathe of awards upon publication, including the Miles Franklin in 1992, and has been a staple of Australian English literature classes for decades. It’s sold hundreds of thousands of copies in Australia alone.

Cloudstreet has topped previous polls on Australian books, including one by the Australian Society of Authors surveying writers on their favourites in 2003, and a subsequent poll run by the ABC the same year, surveying the public. Winton’s novel appeared in a 2019 BBC list of “100 novels that shaped our world”.

The final top 100 in this year’s ABC Radio National poll included adult fiction, nonfiction, young adult fiction, children’s picture books, history and cookbooks.

The Australian Women’s Weekly Children’s Birthday Cake Book made it into the top 50 (at No 22), while Stephanie Alexander’s The Cook’s Companion came in at number 56. RecipeTin Eats: Dinner by Nagi Maehashi made the cut at 96.

Authors Helen Garner, Melissa Lucashenko, Geraldine Brooks, Anna Funder, Peter Carey and Hannah Kent all had multiple books in Sunday’s top 100. Books by children’s authors Alison Lester, Paul Jennings, Mem Fox, Jeannie Baker and Ruth Park appeared in the final 100.

The earliest published work was For the Term of His Natural Life by Marcus Clarke from 1874 (No 80). The most recent were Sally Hepworth’s Mad Mabel and Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore, both published in 2025.

Kate Evans, the host of ABC Radio National’s literary show The Bookshelf, said the list included “audacious literary fiction to historical accounts of who we’ve been and how we might understand all that complicated past, to joyful children’s books, Indigenous stories of both pain and humour, and many, many family stories”.

“This list defies any glib conclusions about how we read – and surely that’s the point,” Evans said.

australia.title: Indigenous woman shackled to hospital bed while in labour in Queensland
australia.snippet: Birth happens days before Labor and Coalition block bill to ban ‘barbaric practice’ of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth Get...
australia.content:
An incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend, an advocacy group has said.

The birth happened just days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a bill to ban the “barbaric practice” of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth.

Debbie Kilroy, the chief executive officer of advocacy group Sisters Inside, said an Aboriginal woman who gave birth via caesarean section to a premature baby on the weekend and was still in hospital had been “shackled on and off since she came into the hospital”.

Hospital staff rang Sisters Inside after trying everything they could to get the shackles removed, she said.

“They were even crying because prison staff wouldn’t remove the shackles.”

A Queensland corrective services spokesperson said the incident would be reviewed.

“This incident will be subject to an internal review as restraints are only ever to be used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners where necessary to maintain public safety,” the spokesperson said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Lidia Thorpe, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman and independent senator for Victoria, introduced bills to the Senate this week to ban shackling and to stop children being strip-searched.

“[The] people sitting in this room have the power to end these barbaric, inhumane, traumatic and totally unnecessary practices,” Thorpe said.

As part of the UN, Australia has signed on to the Bangkok rules on the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”.

But the government said this week the criminal justice system was a matter for the states and territories while the Coalition said it understood the intent of the bill but would not support its passage.

The Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr broke ranks to say he was “deeply concerned” about the practice and would raise it with the Queensland attorney general.

Kilroy said the woman in the Queensland hospital had been “spiralling” before the shackles were removed on Friday.

“As soon as she was shackled her health was deteriorating,” she said.

“Mum wasn’t running anywhere, mum wasn’t being violent.”

An inquiry into Thorpe’s bill heard about women having one leg and one arm shackled, with only one arm available to hold their newborn.

Thorpe said on Friday that “the Albanese government had the opportunity to take a stand against this barbaric practice”.

“Instead, they voted to allow it to continue. Not a day later, we hear of another harrowing case,” she said.

Thorpe said it was “a joke” for the commonwealth to leave it to states and territories because they “have the constitutional power to establish a national standard and they are choosing not to use it”.

“Instead they continue to handball this issue to jurisdictions that have repeatedly failed to stop it,” she said.

“How many more women and their babies have to go through this horrific experience before the Albanese government acts?”

australia.title: Ebike rider, 13, charged with sexual touching after girls and women allegedly harassed on northern beaches
australia.snippet: Sydney teenager charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 t...
australia.content:
An ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged with multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches.

New South Wales police said the boy was arrested on Saturday evening after a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area in the first weeks of October.

“Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm yesterday,” police said on Sunday.

The teenager was taken to Manly police station and charged with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner in or near a public place, and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent.

On Saturday, police had released CCTV images of a male they believed could assist with inquiries.

Police allege that 11 separate incidents occurred against girls and women aged between 13 and 54.

The investigation was initially launched after three separate alleged incidents on 7 and 8 October.

“In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an ebike,” police said on Saturday. In one of the incidents, the offender allegedly made “inappropriate sexual comments”.

At Narrabeen lagoon about 4.30pm on 1 October the suspect “allegedly sexually touched [a] woman before riding away on an ebike,” police said.

Last Monday, police received a further report that between 5pm and 5.30pm that day, two women walking along the Narrabeen lagoon near Bilarong reserve had been sexually touched by a male riding an ebike.

Strike Force Mexvo was established to investigate the incidents with assistance from state crime command’s sex crimes quad.

Speaking in Narrabeen before Saturday’s arrest, Supt John Duncan urged members of the public to come forward with any information about the alleged incidents.

“It’s a bushland park that runs 8km, a large amount of which … runs through bushland, obviously there’s not a great deal of CCTV and cameras.”

The 13-year-old was granted conditional bail to appear at children’s court on 4 November.

australia.title: ‘The strategy is to humiliate’: influencers and the ethics of ‘rage-bait machine’ street interviews
australia.snippet: Influencers from anti-abortion campaigners to anti-immigration activists are making online content out of interactions with Australians o...
australia.content:
“She just kind of appeared in front of me … then she asked if I thought the unborn were human,” Emma Carson says.

Carson was walking through Rundle Mall in Adelaide and thought the woman who approached her was a journalism student or a researcher.

She didn’t realise she was talking to Elspeth Mackellar, one of six content creators at Bird Flip, an organisation pledged to “end abortion”.

They conduct “street interviews”, a popular format on social media that can involve genuine interaction. However, experts say some influencers are using them as “rage bait”, ridiculing or enraging people to get more clicks, and that they operate in a grey legal area if explicit consent to record and publish has not been obtained.

In the clip of Carson, MacKellar holds a small microphone while the cameraperson is off to the side.

Carson says she was taken aback by the approach and Mackellar’s “Gish gallop”, a tactic where interviewees are bombarded with a stream of questions that may lack logic and include misinformation.

“It was only once she asked if the unborn were human that I noticed the person with a camera. I knew if I kept talking, she would continue to find ways to twist my words,” she says.

Carson ended the interview but was worried about how the clip would appear on social media and was angry about the tactic.

“The thing that irks me about people who do this rage-baiting stuff, accost people, blindside them, they don’t want a proper debate because it would wipe out the points they want to make,” she says.

“The strategy is to just humiliate people who disagree with them.”

Rage baiting is online content “deliberately designed to elicit anger or outrage by being frustrating, provocative or offensive, typically posted in order to increase traffic to or engagement with a particular webpage or social media content”, according to the Oxford English Dictionary’s publisher.

There are plenty of other tactics being used by Australian influencers. Some approach demonstrators at pro-Palestine protests, anti-One Nation and anti-March for Australia protests. They then often publish short clips of the protesters looking angry and dishevelled.

Others have set up tables or signs to stage “prove me wrong” scenarios, a tactic popularised by the late US far-right activist Charlie Kirk. Often, the well-rehearsed influencers will post content showing them “demolishing” their detractors.

Other examples include evangelical Christians choosing to preach or to try to debate religion with Muslims, including during Ramadan.

The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman-Grant, said last year there were “growing concerns” about street interviews that “appeared to exploit or humiliate” people, including homeless, drunk or drug-affected people, the West Australian reported.

“Just because something may be technically legal does not mean it is ethical,” she said.

Dr Lisa Harrison, a media and communications lecturer at Flinders Unversity, said the ethics behind street interviews were “really disappointing”. “They’re jumping on controversial topics. You have to wonder if it’s about the controversy or the content,” she said, adding there were also multiple ways to make money out of such content.

She lists advertising, endorsements, paid appearances, sales and fundraising as some of the potential commercial benefits.

“And there’s a lot of ego involved in this,” she says.

In a typical interaction, MacKellar asks people if they believe in human rights then claims it is “hypocritical” to believe in both human rights and abortion.

In fact, international human rights laws protect the right to safe abortions, and do not apply to the unborn.

Prudence Flowers, Flinders University senior lecturer in US history, says in the US, rage-baiting street interviews about abortion have been popular for a while, and her work has shown an increasing crossover between anti-abortion, anti-LGBTQ+ and anti-immigration groups.

She says it is starting to become normalised that someone “might bound up to you and ask questions” before publishing the responses. But she warns that people have no control once the footage is posted and that engaging with street interviews is “just making money for someone else”.

“Everything is content,” she says.

‘Rage baiting’ potential risks

Rage-baiting street interviews can, according to one expert, potentially push beyond questions of ethics and ego and into a more murky legal terrain.

David Vaile, a University of New South Wales privacy and data protection researcher and the former chair of the Australian Privacy Foundation, says the “rage-bait machine” risks breaching a range of state and federal laws including the surveillance devices act, privacy laws, defamation laws, and potentially stalking and harassment laws.

“To the extent the recording starts or continues without the person being aware it’s going on, that may trigger the breach of the Surveillance Devices Act,” he said.

Privacy laws, he said, also meant people should get consent for recording – but complaints often ended up in a “black hole”, and along with other laws were often ambiguous, and weakly or rarely enforced.

Publishing a video of someone else in “bad faith” and painting a false picture that casts that person in a bad light could be a defamation risk, or a breach of stalking and harassment laws if someone was targeted repeatedly, he said.

“And the more you disclose it or broadcast or publish it, that may be a further separate offence from the bare recording,” he said.

MacKellar did not respond to a request for comment.

world.title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
world.snippet: Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds For the 2015 fresh...
world.content:
For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.

Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.

These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.

Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.

The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.

A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.

Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.

Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.

Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.

Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.

“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”

world.title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria
world.snippet: A girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial mon...
world.content:
When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.

Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.

But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.

Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.

“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.

The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.

Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.

Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.

In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.

Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.

Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.

This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”

Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.

Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.

Lovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”

Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.

For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.

“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.

Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.

Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.

Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.

“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.

“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”

world.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
world.snippet: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced ...
world.content:
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.

“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.

The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.

LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.

The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.

The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.

There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean ...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.

She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”

Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”

Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.

“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”

Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

world.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
world.snippet: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approve...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.

She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.

“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.

It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”

When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”

The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.

Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”

It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.

Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.
